scenario: All 3 papers today come from RecSys 2026 and deal with offline evaluation that disagrees with online results. Google Discover ads weight the conversion model's loss by advertiser bids so offline metrics follow advertiser value. A paper from Amazon Music improves how old logs are used to evaluate a new ranking policy, relying less on an assumed chance that each position is seen. Intuit's open-source scikit-rec gives five kinds of recommenders one evaluation interface.

papers.title: A Framework for Value-Aligned Modeling and Robust Experimentation
papers.authors: Krishna Harsha Reddy Kothapalli, Angela Liu, Kamal Nayan Reddy Challa, Pavithra Seshadrivijayakrishnan, Yongpeng Yang, Mustafa Ispir
papers.summary: In the Google Discover ads team's model iteration, offline and online results did not line up. The correlation between the change in the conversion model's offline loss and online advertiser value was only 0.1, and many changes that looked better offline failed in the small-traffic A/B stage. This paper weights the offline loss by how much each click is worth to the advertiser, so that a loss decrease corresponds to a value increase. After the changes, the offline-to-online correlation rose to 0.65, and switching two models to the new objective raised online value by 4.7% in total.
papers.abstract: This industrial framework aligns recommendation-model evaluation with business value across offline, low-traffic online, and high-traffic online experiments. A weighted offline objective improves Delivered Value by 4.7%, raises offline-to-low-traffic correlation from 0.1 to 0.65, and bias controls raise low-to-high-traffic correlation from 0.53 to 0.93. Results cover more than 100 experiments in conversion and click prediction and report a twofold engineering-productivity improvement.

deep_reading.title: A Framework for Value-Aligned Modeling and Robust Experimentation
deep_reading.content:
The Google Discover ads team iterates on models in three steps: compare the loss of the new and old models offline, run a small-traffic A/B to see the value delivered to advertisers, and finally bundle the changes that pass into a large-traffic launch. The old problem was that these three steps did not line up: the correlation between the change in the conversion model's (pConvs) offline Poisson loss and online value was only 0.1, and many changes that looked better offline failed in the small-traffic stage; the correlation between small-traffic and large-traffic results was only 0.53. This paper (RecSys 2026 Best Industry Paper) fixes both ends: ==the offline loss is weighted by how much each click is worth to the advertiser, so that a loss decrease corresponds to a value increase==; on the experimentation side, systematic biases and noise are removed one by one. After the changes, the offline-to-online correlation rose to 0.65 and small-to-large traffic to 0.93, switching two models to the new objective raised online value by 4.7% in total, and the authors estimate that R&D efficiency roughly doubled.

## 1. Three stages, three kinds of error

![The full flow of one model launch. The three stages, left to right, are offline experiments, small-traffic online experiments, and bundled launch; the diamonds are each stage's decision points, and any step that turns out worse sends the change back to an earlier stage. The bottom of each stage marks its time cost O(X), O(Y), O(Z), getting longer and more expensive further along.](figs/recsys26-value-aligned/fig1.jpg)

The auction ranking stage has two models: pCTR predicts the click after an impression, pConvs predicts the number of conversions after a click; together with the advertiser's bid they produce the auction score for a second-price auction. The business metric behind launch decisions is Delivered Value (DV):

$$DV=\sum_{i\in \text{Clicks}}T_i\cdot C_i$$

$T_i$ is the target price per conversion the advertiser is willing to pay (tCPA), $C_i$ is the number of conversions from the $i$-th click. A purchase of a 1,000-dollar mattress is worth more than a hundred visits to a merchant's website, yet an ordinary conversion prediction loss counts both as equal conversions.

The stages take O(X), O(Y) and O(Z) time respectively, with X much smaller than Y and Y much smaller than Z, so every wrong judgment in an earlier stage wastes the more expensive resources of later stages. The authors split measurement error into three kinds: objective misalignment (what an earlier stage measures does not predict the later stage's result), systematic error (bias introduced by the experimental setup), and random error (variance from system noise).

## 2. Aligning the offline loss with delivered value

### 2.1 pConvs: Poisson loss weighted by tCPA

pConvs originally did maximum likelihood under a Poisson distribution, with the Poisson loss (PL) $PL=\sum_i P_i-C_i\log P_i$, where $P_i$ is the predicted number of conversions for the $i$-th click. The model's output does not change: it still predicts conversions per click. What changes is the loss, which multiplies each click by the advertiser's value per conversion $T_i$, giving the weighted Poisson loss (WPL). Mistakes on high-value clicks now cost more, so the model is effectively fitting delivered value $T_i\cdot C_i$ rather than conversion counts:

$$WPL=\sum_{i\in \text{Clicks}}T_i\,\big[P_i-C_i\log P_i\big]$$

The paper gives a derivation for why the weighting is correct. Let the advertiser's true value be $v=T_iC_i$, the bid $b=T_iP_i$, and the second price (what the advertiser actually pays) $s$ have density $f(s)$; the expected profit of one auction is the integral of "value minus cost" over winning outcomes, $\int_0^b (v-s)f(s)\,ds$. If $f(s)\propto 1/s$, the integral comes out as $v\ln b-b$ plus a constant, so maximizing profit is equivalent to minimizing $b-v\ln b$; substituting $b$ and $v$ back and dropping parameter-independent constants gives WPL. Poisson regression works here ==not because conversion counts really follow a Poisson distribution, but because the 1/s cost distribution approximately holds==.

### 2.2 pCTR: from "whether clicked" to "how many clicks"

pCTR originally predicted the probability that an impression is clicked at least once, trained with log loss and evaluated with AUCLoss (1 minus AUC). A carousel ad impression often gets several clicks, and each extra click has value, so the team changed the target to the expected number of clicks per impression, raising online DV by 1.2%.

This change is almost invisible offline:

| Offline metric | Change |
|---|---|
| Binary AUCLoss | -0.10% |
| Multi-class AUCLoss | -0.15% |
| LL | +0.08% |
| PL_CTR | -0.21% |

Log loss even got worse; only the Poisson loss computed on click counts, PL_CTR, dropped clearly, matching the direction of the 1.2% online gain.

pCTR also needs to carry value, but using conversion value directly as the weight fails because too few clicks have conversions and the labels are an order of magnitude sparser. The authors instead use expected delivered value (EDV) as a proxy: for every actual click, multiply the value per conversion $T_i$ by the pConvs model's predicted conversions and sum, $EDV=\sum_{i\in\text{clicks}} T_i\cdot pConvs_i$. The pCTR model trains on every impression, clicked or not. Each impression is weighted by an estimate of the value one click would bring: the ad's value per conversion $T_j$ times the pConvs model's predicted conversions per click $pConvs_j$, shared by all clicks in that impression, giving $WPL_{CTR}=\sum_j T_j\,pConvs_j\,[P_j-Y_j\log P_j]$, where $Y_j$ is the number of clicks on the $j$-th impression. The appendix uses the assumption that the runner-up's effective cost-per-thousand-impressions bid follows a $1/r$ distribution to give a derivation of the same form as 2.1.

### 2.3 Results after switching objectives

This experiment is meant to show two things: WPL as an offline metric better predicts online value, and training on WPL directly raises value.

| Model | PL change | WPL change | Online DV |
|---|---|---|---|
| pConvs trained on WPL | +0.1% | -0.35% | +3% |
| pCTR trained on WPL | +0.03% | -0.04% | +0.5% |

For both models PL got worse, WPL got better, and online DV went up, which shows that what PL measures points in a different direction from the business objective.

The authors measure how good an offline metric is by correlation: over the same set of changes, compute the Pearson correlation between the change in the offline metric and the change in online DV (absolute values are reported below). For pConvs, over about 40 experiments with online data, the old PL is almost uncorrelated with online value (0.1), while WPL reaches 0.65 and stays around 0.69 on later new experiments, which shows the result was not picked after the fact. pCTR is similar: the original AUCLoss and log loss are essentially uncorrelated with online value (0.16 and 0.09), and after switching to expected clicks and evaluating with $WPL_{CTR}$, the correlation rises to 0.63.

![Scatter plots of pCTR experiments' offline metric against online EDV, one point per experiment. In the left plot the x-axis is AUCLoss and the fitted line is almost flat, correlation 0.16; in the right plot the x-axis is WPL and the points follow a downward fitted line, correlation 0.63: the lower the offline loss, the higher the online value.](figs/recsys26-value-aligned/fig2.jpg)

## 3. Offline stage: systematic and random error

All models are trained continuously online, each example passes through only once, and offline evaluation uses progressive validation: each example is first predicted and its loss recorded, then used for training.

Systematic error has two sources. The first is label maturity bias. Conversion labels arrive with delay, and the experiment model starts later than the control, so while catching up on historical data it sees more complete conversion labels. Its loss over the same time period then looks better only because it has more information. The fix is to compare only over periods where the two models' training data have the same quality. The second is optimizer and architecture artifacts. Architectures like DLRM first split features into groups and then let features interact within a group. Adding even one constant feature, which carries no information, can shift the grouping and split important features that need to interact into different groups, causing a systematic regression. The paper also lists second-order optimizers as a source of such artifacts but does not explain how they cause it; the authors' remedy is one principle: in architectures that group features, watch whether correlated features end up in the same group. The paper gives no concrete procedure. After fixing these two, the offline difference between two equivalent models stays within 0.02%, where previously significant differences were often measured.

Random error is suppressed by standardizing the measurement method. The table below compares, over 25 pConvs experiments, the offline-online correlation and the AUC-ROC of using the offline result to judge whether the online result is good, when the offline metric is measured over different time windows. $T$ is each experiment's launch time.

| Offline measurement window | Correlation | AUC-ROC |
|---|---|---|
| [T−6 months, T−3 months] | 0.650 | 0.760 |
| [T−1 month, T] | 0.577 | 0.690 |
| [T−1 week, T] | 0.01 | 0.489 |
| Same fixed 3 months for all experiments | 0.640 | 0.755 |
| [T, T+online experiment duration] | 0.604 | 0.736 |

Looking only at the last week, offline results have almost no predictive power: the correlation is close to 0 and AUC-ROC is even below 0.5, worse than random guessing; a 3-month window beats a 1-month one, because the longer the window, the more random noise averages out. WPL weights range from a few cents to over a thousand dollars and are very noisy. So during measurement the weights get an upper limit, with anything above it counted at the limit; the limit matches the one used for DV capping below (the paper does not publish the value), which halves the confidence interval without introducing bias.

## 4. Online stage: the small-traffic control must be as small as the experiment

### 4.1 Systematic error comes from different traffic sizes

The common practice is to compare the small-traffic experiment model against the large-traffic production model, which is necessarily biased. There are three reasons. The first is the winner's curse. In an auction, ads whose value is overestimated are more likely to win, and a model corrects this bias in continuous training from the impressions and conversions its own winning bids bring back. A small-traffic model wins few impressions with its own bids, so it lacks the feedback to correct itself; a large-traffic model has plenty of such data. The second is budget. A campaign's budget is fixed and does not scale with experiment traffic. Take a campaign with a $100 budget that the experiment nearly exhausts at small traffic. At large traffic the impressions grow but the budget is still $100, so the extra impressions cannot be bought and the gain seen at small traffic shrinks. Small traffic therefore overestimates value. The paper notes that parallel split-budget experiments can mitigate this but are not practical. The third is feedback loops. At large traffic, feedback loops keep correcting deviations in predictions so that delivery meets its target constraints. At small traffic the data are too sparse, and running a separate feedback loop would hurt, so this correction is missing. The paper does not say which metrics the target constraints refer to.

The authors' approach is to set a standard small-traffic size and retrain a copy of the production model at that traffic size, as a shared control for all experiments of that size. When another traffic size is needed, a separate control of that size is trained. After the change, the DV difference between two identical retrained models is close to 0%, where it used to often exceed 1%.

![Scatter comparison of small-traffic and large-traffic results; the x-axis is DV measured at small traffic, the y-axis DV measured at large traffic. Red diamonds and the dashed line are the old setup, green dots and the solid line are after using the fixed retrained control. Axis values are hidden for confidentiality, with equal steps per grid cell. The green dots sit closer to their trend line, and the trend line is closer to 45 degrees, showing that gains measured at small traffic replicate better at large traffic.](figs/recsys26-value-aligned/fig3.jpg)

This comparison uses 7 historical experiments (old setup) and 8 new experiments (new setup); the small-to-large traffic correlation rose from 0.53 to 0.93. The sample is small because large-traffic experiments are expensive, but each large-traffic experiment runs long with a lot of traffic, so each single measurement is itself precise. The two correlations, 0.53 and 0.93, cannot be compared as independent measurements: the paper says both setups evaluate the same underlying models, so the two sets of measurements are themselves correlated, at about 0.75. The paper does not say how the 7 and 8 experiments correspond or how the 0.75 was computed. The authors compare the two dependent correlations with a Williams t-test and find the rise from 0.53 to 0.93 significant (p<0.05).

### 4.2 Random error: capping and expected values

DV depends on sparse conversions, so its confidence interval is wide, and the authors narrow it in two ways. First, capping per-click values shrinks the interval width by 40%. Second, replacing actual DV with expected DV (pConvs predictions in place of actual conversions) shrinks the width by 70%. Both move the measured DV away from its unprocessed value; the paper's Table 5 lists this cost as under 3% and about 5% without saying what the percentages are relative to, and the text says the effect on metric bias is marginal. Combined, a 2%-traffic experiment reaches the precision of a former 30%-traffic experiment, ==so the same traffic can run more experiments in parallel==.

## 5. Why correlation determines efficiency

The authors assume that offline and online results follow a correlated bivariate normal distribution; multiplying the probability that the offline judgment agrees in direction with the next stage by the probability that the small-traffic judgment agrees with large traffic gives the probability that both judgments are correct:

$$P_{good}=\Big[\tfrac12+\tfrac{\arcsin(\rho_{off})}{\pi}\Big]\cdot\Big[\tfrac12+\tfrac{\arcsin(\rho_{on})}{\pi}\Big]$$

$\rho_{off}$ is the offline-to-small-traffic correlation and $\rho_{on}$ the small-to-large traffic correlation. With the pre-improvement values, the probability that both judgments are right is only about 0.36, meaning most changes were misjudged at one step or the other; with the post-improvement values, it rises to about 0.65.

![Heatmap of the probability of making the right decision as a function of the two correlations; the x-axis is the offline correlation, the y-axis the online correlation, and greener means higher probability. The bottom-left point (0.1, 0.53) is before the improvements, the top-right point (0.69, 0.93) after.](figs/recsys26-value-aligned/fig4.jpg)

The text gives the improved offline correlation as 0.65 while the figure marks 0.69, but by the formula the two correspond to probabilities only about 0.01 apart, so the conclusion is unaffected. The paper's efficiency evidence is 100+ experimental changes over 3 years: the number of successful changes included in each bundled pConvs launch, and the number of changes per contributor, both kept rising. The authors estimate overall efficiency roughly doubled, with exact numbers withheld for confidentiality.

## 6. Limitations

The authors acknowledge that all evidence comes from a single continuously trained online environment, Google Discover ads. The WPL derivation relies on costs following a $1/s$ distribution; the authors note in the appendix that the actual runner-up bid distribution decays faster with a lighter tail, and leave cost distributions closer to reality for future work.

In addition, DV itself is a simplified metric the paper uses to illustrate the problem; real launches look at several interdependent metrics, and the small-to-large traffic correlation is based on only 7 and 8 experiments.

## 7. Practical implications

- If your model serves an auction ranked by bids, try multiplying the offline evaluation loss by each example's business value and check whether its correlation with online results improves; without changing training, this tells you whether your current offline metric is measuring the wrong thing.
- A small-traffic experiment's control should be the same size and retrained the same way as the experiment arm. Comparing a small-traffic experiment arm against the large-traffic production model mixes winner's curse, budget and feedback-control biases into the measured difference, and an A/A experiment can catch this first.

deep_reading.title: scikit-rec: A Unified, Extensible Recommendation Library with scikit-rec-agent, a Conversational Interface
deep_reading.content:
When a recommendation team maintains ranking models, contextual bandits, uplift models and sequential recommenders at the same time, it usually ends up with one library for matrix factorization, another for bandits, another for sequential models, and a separate set of glue code for evaluation, each with its own interface. To compare a ranking policy against a bandit policy on the same logs, the team has to make sure both sides are evaluated the same way by hand. Intuit's open-source scikit-rec puts all of this in one library: every recommendation pipeline is split into three layers, Recommender, Scorer and Estimator, and five recommendation paradigms share one evaluate(), which includes six off-policy evaluators plus an on-policy baseline. Its IPS, SNIPS, DR and DM estimates differ from the Open Bandit Pipeline (OBP) reference implementations by at most 4×10⁻¹⁶ relative. The companion scikit-rec-agent uses 15 structured tools to turn a plain-English description of data and goals into a trained, evaluated pipeline. An internal version has run at Intuit for 3+ years, powering 15 use cases across TurboTax and QuickBooks under a real-time latency requirement below 100 ms. ==The paper's contribution is a unified evaluation standard, not model accuracy==, and the authors state explicitly that the experiments only serve to show the implementation is correct.

## 1. What existing libraries lack

The paper's Table 1 lists nine mainstream open-source frameworks. RecBole has 94 algorithms but only supports standard held-out evaluation; OBP only does off-policy evaluation for bandits and has no recommendation pipeline; Vowpal Wabbit supports contextual bandits and counterfactual evaluation, also without a recommendation pipeline; Merlin, TorchRec and TFRS focus on retrieval and ranking on GPUs. The authors conclude that no library puts ranking, bandits, uplift and sequential recommendation in one pipeline and compares them with one set of counterfactual evaluators.

Why not extend a framework like RecBole? The authors' reason is that those frameworks are organized around a fixed model catalog, so adding a new paradigm touches many places; in scikit-rec, a new paradigm is just one Recommender subclass.

## 2. The three layers

![scikit-rec's three-layer structure. The top layer, Recommender, holds business logic and strategy, with six types: ranking, uplift, multi-objective GCSL (goal-conditioned supervised learning: the desired value of each objective is fed in as a condition, trained with the outcomes actually reached and served with the targets one wants), contextual bandits, sequential and hierarchical sequential; the middle layer, Scorer, decides how items are scored, with seven types; the bottom layer, Estimator, is the machine-learning model, in tabular, embedding and sequential families. During training, train() and fit() are called top-down; at inference, predict() and recommend() return bottom-up. The dashed box at the bottom notes that any layer can be swapped on its own: changing the Estimator never requires touching the Scorer or Recommender.](figs/recsys26-scikit-rec/fig1.jpg)

The **Estimator** is the underlying model, in three families. Tabular: XGBoost, LightGBM, sklearn models, and a pure-NumPy matrix factorization (ALS or SGD, no PyTorch needed). Embedding: MF, NCF, Two-Tower, NFM, DCN, DeepFM. Sequential: SASRec and HRNN (a hierarchical recurrent network: user history is cut into sessions, a lower GRU reads the items within a session, and an upper GRU chains the sessions in order to carry memory across them), both of which need PyTorch.

The **Scorer** decides how candidate items are scored for a user context. The most common is UniversalScorer: one global model whose input includes item features. IndependentScorer instead trains a separate model per item. There are also multiclass (items as mutually exclusive classes), multi-output (one label column per item, each binary or regression), mixed-type multi-target (targets of different types, such as binary, regression and multiclass, in one model), sequential (for SASRec) and hierarchical (for HRNN) scorers, seven in total.

The **Recommender** is the business-logic layer, one per paradigm: deterministic ranking (with optional temperature sampling), contextual bandits (two strategies: epsilon-greedy; and static action, which always recommends a preset list of items without model scoring, documented as a control group for A/B tests), uplift (treatment-effect estimation with T/S/X-Learners), SASRec-based sequential recommendation, and HRNN-based hierarchical sequential recommendation.

Once the contracts between layers are fixed, swapping XGBoost for a Two-Tower model is a one-line config change, with the Scorer and Recommender untouched. The data side is unified into three tables too, interactions, users and items, each declared by a YAML schema of required columns, dtypes and outcome fields, and validated at construction time.

## 3. One evaluate() over seven evaluators

This layer answers how policies from different paradigms can be compared fairly on the same logs. Logs are produced by the old online policy (the logging policy), and many items a new policy would recommend were never shown, so they have no real feedback. Off-policy evaluation (OPE) uses the old policy's logs to estimate how a new policy would perform online. The most basic estimator, IPS (inverse propensity scoring), is:

$$\hat{V}_{IPS}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\pi(a_i\mid x_i)}{\pi_0(a_i\mid x_i)}\,r_i$$

$x_i$ is the context of log entry $i$, $a_i$ is the item shown at the time, $r_i$ is the feedback received, $\pi_0$ is the old policy's probability of choosing that item (the propensity), and $\pi$ is the new policy's probability of choosing it. Intuitively, the more a new policy favors items the old policy rarely chose, the larger the weight on those samples.

| Evaluator | Type | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| SimpleEvaluator | On-policy | Held-out test set, same policy |
| ReplayMatchEvaluator | Off-policy | Conservative; matched actions only |
| IPSEvaluator | Off-policy | Different policy; needs propensities |
| DREvaluator | Off-policy | Doubly robust; lower variance than IPS |
| SNIPSEvaluator | Off-policy | Self-normalized IPS |
| PolicyWeightedEvaluator | Off-policy | Assumes a uniform logging policy; weights rewards by the new policy's probability for the item, divided by that probability's global mean |
| DirectMethodEvaluator | Off-policy | Reward model; no propensities needed |

The seven evaluators pair with twelve metrics (Precision, Recall, MAP, MRR, NDCG@k, ROC-AUC, Expected Reward and others). Recommendation scores are cached internally, so switching metrics or top-k cutoffs needs no new inference.

## 4. scikit-rec-agent: the LLM configures, it is not the model

![scikit-rec-agent's system structure. In the middle is the agent loop, which calls the LLM, dispatches tools, runs safety checks and keeps session history; on the left is the pluggable LLM interface, supporting Anthropic, OpenAI and custom adapters; on the right are the 15 tools, in three groups for data handling, training and diagnosis, and evaluation and comparison, which finally call scikit-rec's pipeline factory; session state holds only handles to datasets and models; at the bottom are the two hallucination checks that run every turn.](figs/recsys26-scikit-rec/fig2.jpg)

Choosing the Recommender, Scorer, Estimator, evaluator and data split takes a fair amount of domain knowledge. scikit-rec-agent wraps the whole workflow as a conversation: loading data, validating schemas, splitting, training, diagnosing failures, comparing many methods in a batch, tuning hyperparameters and saving models, 15 tools in all. A few design details:

- Datasets and models in session state are indexed by ID; only metadata enters the LLM context, never Python objects.
- "Which pipeline to recommend" is not a tool. The LLM gives 2–5 config dicts with rationales directly in its reply for the user to pick from, and config validity is checked by the pipeline factory, so the decision stays in the auditable conversation record.
- Two deterministic checks run on every output: a URL-echo check flags links the user never supplied and the system prompt does not contain; a foreign-reference check uses an AST scan of code blocks to flag imports outside the trusted set. Warnings are not written into conversation history, so the LLM cannot learn to evade them.

==Every pipeline it produces is an ordinary scikit-rec composition, and the LLM takes no part in online scoring==. In regulated settings where opaque model decisions are not allowed, this keeps every produced model auditable and reproducible. The preliminary evaluation is rough: on 5 internal Intuit datasets and 5 public ones, every pipeline the agent produced ran end to end, as checked separately by two authors by hand with full agreement; in an informal 20-prompt probe, the URL-echo check caught 5 non-existent links the LLM made up.

## 5. Design choices driven by production

Section 5 of the paper describes several design choices worked back from Intuit's production use cases:

- **Scorer as its own layer**. QuickBooks moved from "one propensity model per product" to a unified next-best-action recommender; the two setups differ only at the scoring layer, IndependentScorer versus UniversalScorer. The migration only swapped the Scorer argument, leaving the Recommender, Estimator and evaluation code untouched.
- **recommend_online**. The standard recommend() does a pandas merge across the interactions, users and items DataFrames, which is fine for batch scoring, but TurboTax's single-user real-time requests have a budget below 100 ms and the join overhead dominates. recommend_online skips the merge, takes pre-split single-row inputs, and goes through a NumPy-only scoring path.
- **XGBoost latency**. The default predict_proba builds a new DMatrix on every call, validates feature names, and copies the input into contiguous memory. XGBClassifierEstimator converts to NumPy once, uses Booster.inplace_predict() to avoid the copy, and turns off feature validation (features were already validated at the schema stage).

## 6. Experiments: proving correctness, not competing on accuracy

The first experiment checks accuracy on MovieLens-1M, to show that each model's implementation lands in a reasonable range of published results. The protocol follows the NCF and SASRec papers: each user's last behavior is held out and ranked together with 100 random negatives, reporting HR@10 and NDCG@10.

| Model | HR@10 | NDCG@10 | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| BPR-MF (published) | 0.5781 | 0.3287 | Classical CF |
| Caser (published) | 0.7886 | 0.5538 | CNN sequential |
| SASRec original (published) | 0.8245 | 0.5905 | Reference impl. |
| MF-ALS (pure NumPy) | 0.7931 | 0.5421 | No PyTorch |
| SASRec (BCE) | 0.8953 | 0.6331 | Positives only |
| SASRec (MSE, ratings) | 0.8741 | 0.6102 | Soft labels |
| HRNN hierarchical sequential | 0.8612 | 0.5988 | Two-level GRU |

scikit-rec's SASRec scores higher than the original, and the authors say plainly that this comes from using only rating ≥4 behaviors as positives, a cleaner sequential signal, not from a method improvement, so the two are not directly comparable. The rows that can be compared directly are the scikit-rec ones, which share identical data preparation, splits and negative sampling.

Another experiment checks that the off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimators have no numerical implementation errors. The data is ZOZOTOWN's Open Bandit Dataset with 80 actions; logs from a random policy are used to estimate the value of a Bernoulli Thompson Sampling policy (BTS, a bandit policy that picks items by sampling from the posterior of each item's click rate), with 20 bootstrap resamples. The dataset was collected by running both policies at the same time on the same recommendation slots, with part of the traffic served by the random policy and part by BTS. The actual mean click rate in BTS's share of the logs is therefore BTS's true value, which can check the estimate computed from the random policy's logs alone. The IPS, SNIPS, DR and DM estimates differ from the OBP reference implementations by at most 4×10⁻¹⁶ relative, that is, only floating-point error, which shows the implementation matches the reference exactly. In the table below, bias is the absolute difference between the mean of the 20 estimates and the true value; relative RMSE is √E[(estimate/true value − 1)²], the error normalized by the true value.

| Estimator | Estimate | Bias | Rel. RMSE |
|---|---|---|---|
| IPS | 0.00417 | 2.6×10⁻⁵ | 0.231 |
| SNIPS | 0.00435 | 1.5×10⁻⁴ | 0.251 |
| DR | 0.00393 | 2.7×10⁻⁴ | 0.221 |
| Replay-Match | 0.00356 | 6.4×10⁻⁴ | 0.196 |

Only a 10K-row sample is used here, so the IPS family's relative RMSE sits around 25%; the authors say the full 26M-row release is needed for tight intervals. ==An OPE implementation bug raises no error; it just quietly picks the wrong policy==, so matching the reference implementation bit for bit is more useful than reporting a nice-looking metric.

## 7. Limitations and what to try

Gaps the authors list: retrieval is still brute force, with no approximate-nearest-neighbor index such as FAISS or ScaNN; bandits have only epsilon-greedy and static-action, no Thompson Sampling or LinUCB; adversarial testing of the agent and a held-out task benchmark are not done yet, and the URL-echo check has known gaps. Also, the uplift paradigm is validated only on synthetic data and the TurboTax production use case; public rating data has no treatment assignment, so the paper has no accuracy numbers for it.

What to try:

- If your team runs ranking and bandit policies side by side, you can use its evaluate() to run IPS, DR and Replay-Match on the same logs and first confirm both sides are evaluated the same way.
- If your team implements its own OPE, you can follow the paper and check your numbers once against OBP bit for bit on the Open Bandit Dataset.

papers.title: Generalized Position-Based Model: Rethinking Position Weights in Ranking Off-Policy Evaluation
papers.authors: Norman Knyazev, Vito Bellini, Huseyin Yurtseven, Ben London
papers.summary: When click logs from an old ranking policy are used to estimate a new policy's clicks, existing methods rely on hand-set rules for how clicks at each position are converted. GPBM learns a weight for every position from the data and is far more accurate when the assumed position bias is wrong. To predict clicks at one position of the new policy, the existing INTERPOL just pools, with equal weight, the logged clicks at positions inside a nearby window whose width must be set in advance. GPBM writes the new policy's click estimate at each position as a weighted sum of logged clicks at all positions, and picks the weights to minimise an upper bound on the error that covers both random noise and the bias from a wrong seen-probability curve. In clicks simulated from expert labels on Yahoo search data, when the assumed curve is too high, its mean squared error is more than 6 times lower than INTERPOL with the window tuned in hindsight.
papers.abstract: Off-policy evaluation for ranked recommendations depends on assumptions about user behavior and position bias. GPBM learns position-specific weights by minimizing an approximate upper bound on estimation error instead of requiring fixed uniform windows. It retains the unbiasedness guarantees of INTERPOL and reports more accurate and robust estimates across position-bias errors, logging policies, and dataset sizes.
